video_title: The U.K. Is Becoming a Poor Country | Sam Bowman
gist: Works in Progress editor Sam Bowman argues Britain is a stagnating catch-up economy suffering ~20 years of zero median wage growth, and that a single keyhole reform - housing supply and the planning regime that throttles it - would unlock enough growth to make every other fix affordable. The conversation runs through the mechanics of stamp duty lock-in, vetocracy, fiscal over-centralisation, social-housing mandates, and closes on why AI's dependence on compute and energy makes Britain's inability to build a direct constraint on its position in the AI era.

themes.theme: Two Lost Decades & the Catch-Up Thesis

insights.claim: Britain is approaching two lost decades with roughly zero median wage growth since around 2008, and Sam Bowman treats the median worker's stagnant wage - not headline GDP - as the definitive marker that the UK is now a poor country.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Anchors UK domestic-demand and consumer-facing equity assumptions to a two-decade real-income flatline rather than to nominal GDP prints.
insights.quote: We are approaching two lost decades, 20 years of basically zero median wage growth

insights.claim: Sam Bowman classifies the UK as a catch-up economy rather than a frontier-innovation economy, arguing most attainable growth comes from adopting practices already proven elsewhere - the mechanism by which Poland tripled wealth per person since the end of communism.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Reframes UK upside as a policy-copying trade with identifiable catalysts, not a speculative bet on domestic innovation or an AI champion emerging.
insights.quote: tripled in wealth per person since the end of communism

insights.claim: Sam Bowman dates Britain's institutional damage to the 1945 Attlee nationalisations, which he says coincided with UK economic performance dropping 10 to 15 percentage points against the US despite Britain being far less physically destroyed than continental Europe.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Implies the UK underperformance gap is institutional and reversible by statute, not a function of geography, capital stock or war damage.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's growth model holds that centralised states almost never generate growth except by removing barriers, while local governments with tax upside reliably can - he cites Manchester's municipal investment in a canal in the 1880s that turned an inland city into Britain's third busiest port.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Sets the test for any UK growth policy: does it move fiscal upside to the level that bears the cost of building?
insights.quote: the third busiest port in Britain

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues China's growth is driven by competition between city governments that capture land-lease and industrial spillovers locally, not by Beijing's top-down direction - a reading he calls completely opposite to the standard Western account and is publishing in Works in Progress.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: If Chinese growth is decentralised competition rather than central planning, top-down Chinese stimulus signals are a weaker read on Chinese activity than local-government land economics.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman is a short-term pessimist and long-term optimist on Britain because the assets that cannot be legislated into existence - rule of law, unusually low political corruption, elite institutions, a culture of open argument - remain intact while the broken parts are all policy-shaped.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Frames UK assets as deeply out-of-favour but with a policy-driven re-rating path, arguing the bear case is cyclical-political rather than structural-institutional.
insights.quote: What we've got wrong are things that we could fix. You and I could fix in 6 months

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's housing theory of everything holds that housing shortages don't merely raise rents but propagate into lower birth rates, lower productivity, less business formation, worse health, higher carbon emissions and widening regional and intergenerational inequality - making housing the upstream variable behind most measured UK problems.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Provides a single leading indicator - housing completions in high-demand cities - for a wide basket of UK macro and demographic trends.

insights.claim: London built roughly 4,000 homes last year against a target of about 80,000, a shortfall of around 95% in the UK's most economically important housing market.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A ~95% miss against target means London supply is effectively fixed, supporting rent inflation and making any credible supply reform a large repricing event for UK housebuilders and land.
insights.quote: we built 4,000 homes last year in London

insights.claim: About 40% of inner London housing is social housing and roughly half of those tenants are retired or otherwise economically inactive, meaning around 20% of inner London's housing stock is occupied by economically inactive people in the most valuable labour market in Western Europe.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Quantifies an allocation problem distinct from the supply problem - a policy lever that could raise London's effective labour supply without building anything.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues housing became an investable asset class only because supply was frozen, so UK housing now trades on the logic of gold or fine art rather than as a durable good where higher prices call forth more production.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Implies UK house prices are a scarcity trade, so the single biggest risk to the asset class is a credible supply-side reform rather than a demand or rate shock.
insights.quote: Housing is like gold or fine art because the supply is so so so scarce

insights.claim: Sam Bowman treats the financialisation of UK property - people buying second and third homes as pension substitutes - as a consequence of fixed supply rather than a cause of the shortage, inverting the common narrative that landlords and investors created the problem.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Predicts that policies attacking landlords will not fix affordability, so investor-targeted measures are political risk without a supply payoff.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's base case is not a nominal UK house price crash but flat nominal and falling real prices, noting the declines so far are concentrated in leasehold flats where the ownership deal has effectively been taxed, while houses have been roughly flat on interest-rate-driven mortgage credit contraction.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Separates the leasehold-flat problem from the broader UK housing market, arguing the real-terms erosion trade is the more likely path than a nominal crash.

insights.claim: Britain has the smallest homes in Western Europe and is one of the only markets where older homes sell at a premium to new-build, which Sam Bowman reads as direct evidence that regulatory and mandated costs are being absorbed through degraded size and quality of new product.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A new-build discount to century-old stock is a measurable signal of regulatory cost pass-through and a quality risk for UK housebuilder brand and pricing power.
insights.quote: new homes are being sold at a discount relative to homes that were built 100 years ago

themes.theme: Stamp Duty, Exit Taxes & Capital Flight

insights.claim: Sam Bowman calls stamp duty the single worst tax in Britain because it raises only around £15bn - trivial beside income tax, VAT and national insurance - while locking households out of moving for work.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A tax with a small revenue base and large behavioural distortion is the most plausible candidate for reform, and abolition would be a step-change catalyst for UK transaction volumes.
insights.quote: stamp duty is the worst tax we've got

insights.claim: George Osborne's stamp duty reform removed the slab-system cliff edges but paid for it with steeply progressive top-end rates, which fall disproportionately on London where most zone-three family homes with more than two bedrooms now exceed £1m.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Explains why transaction friction is worst precisely in the highest-productivity labour market, concentrating the mobility damage where it costs the economy most.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman proposes abolishing stamp duty and replacing it with an annual property tax that only begins when a household moves in, predicting it would be one of the most popular tax rises in history because existing owners pay nothing until they choose to transact.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A politically feasible reform design to watch in UK budgets - it would unlock a wave of deferred housing transactions and associated renovation spend.

insights.claim: The UK-US tax wedge on high earners is now large enough to drive relocation: on a £1m income, take-home is around £541,000 in the UK versus about £588,000 in Los Angeles - a high-tax blue state - and £650,000 to £670,000 in states with no income tax, with US employer payroll taxes also lower.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the arbitrage driving UK high-earner emigration, a structural headwind to the UK income tax base and to domestic consumption at the top end.
insights.quote: if you earn a million pound a year you'll pay

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's principal fiscal-risk call is the combination of an exit tax with a large capital gains tax increase - measures that are politically popular and signal which side a government is on, but raise little revenue while driving asset holders out.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Flags the specific UK budget measures most likely to trigger capital and founder flight, and therefore the key policy event risk for UK-resident asset holders.
insights.quote: an exit tax is a terrible idea

insights.claim: The host frames exit-tax timing as an unhedgeable event risk, noting such a measure could be announced with immediate midnight effect at a budget, leaving UK-resident asset holders trapped with no window to change residency.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Implies that for those weighing UK residency, the option value of moving decays to zero at the budget date rather than at implementation.

themes.theme: Planning, Vetocracy & the Cost of Consent

insights.claim: The planning application for the Lower Thames Crossing tunnel between Essex and Kent ran to 360,000 pages and cost £297m to produce - more than the entire construction cost of the world's longest road tunnel in Norway, for a project that has not yet begun work.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: The single most quotable measure of UK infrastructure consenting costs, and the reason UK infrastructure pipelines carry far higher pre-construction risk capital than peers.
insights.quote: the production of this planning document has cost

insights.claim: Before the 1940s Britain had a planning system, but councils blocking development had to compensate the landowner - so refusal powers were used sparingly, meaning the interwar building boom came from better incentive design rather than from an absence of planning.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Points to a concrete reform template - price the veto - rather than the politically impossible option of abolishing planning.
insights.quote: they bore the costs of stopping you

insights.claim: Britain has never built more houses than it did in the 1930s, almost entirely through private-sector building, and adjusted for population that rate would be about four times current output.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Establishes that a 4x uplift in UK housebuilding is historically demonstrated rather than theoretical, setting the scale of the prize from planning reform.
insights.quote: We have never built more houses than we built in the 1930s

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's vetocracy framework holds that the British state and its regulation are structured so development is win-lose for neighbours, so every affected party rationally acquires a veto and uses it - producing a system in which nothing gets built.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Predicts that reforms which don't create local winners will fail regardless of national mandate - a filter for assessing any UK build-out programme.
insights.quote: Everybody wants a veto. And as a result, nothing happens. Nothing gets built. Vetos are always used.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman identifies the legal blocker to win-win development: the UK planning system is explicitly required to ignore local benefits and treats a developer's offer to share revenue with neighbours as a bribe rather than as compensation.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Identifies a narrow, specific statutory change - allowing benefit-sharing to be a material planning consideration - as a high-leverage unlock for UK development.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues UK housebuilders steer both Conservative and Labour governments toward greenfield land release and away from urban densification, because brownfield liberalisation would invite new entrants and competition into markets the incumbents currently dominate.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Suggests listed UK housebuilders are structurally aligned against the reform with the largest economic payoff - and would be the relative losers if urban densification ever passed.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues mandated social-housing quotas of 30% to 50% on new developments function as a large tax levied specifically on the one activity policy claims to want more of, and are a bigger constraint on building than planning in some places.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Identifies affordable-housing mandates as a direct, quantifiable margin drag on UK development viability that is rarely priced as a tax.
insights.quote: It's a gigantic tax on new building

insights.claim: Because buyers face a fixed budget constraint, Sam Bowman argues every increase in mandated development cost is absorbed through smaller and lower-quality new homes rather than through developer margin or lower land prices.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Explains why UK new-build quality declines as affordability policy tightens - a reputational and regulatory risk building in the housebuilder sector.

insights.claim: Central Manchester's residential renaissance came from the council setting a 0% social-housing requirement rather than the 20% then standard, on the explicit reasoning that a 20% requirement would have delivered zero units because nothing would have been built.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A live UK natural experiment showing quota removal, not quota enforcement, is what actually delivers urban housing volume.
insights.quote: if we required 20% social housing, we wouldn't get 20% social housing. We get zero

insights.claim: Estate regeneration is a working win-win template in London: the Aberfeldy Village scheme in Poplar would add roughly 2,500 units plus about 100 additional socially rented homes while replacing all existing social units, and the resident ballot drew 94% turnout with 92% voting in favour.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that near-unanimous local consent for dense development is obtainable when residents capture the upside - a replicable model for UK urban density plays.
insights.quote: It had 94% turnout and 92% of the residents were in favor

insights.claim: Roughly 96% of UK tax revenue flows through Whitehall - against a figure discussed as around 40% retained locally in Switzerland - so local authorities capture almost none of the tax generated by development in their area and are structurally near-bankrupt.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Quantifies why UK local opposition to building is economically rational, and marks fiscal devolution as the precondition for any national build-out.
insights.quote: It's 96%. Our councils are broke.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's core reform is letting local authorities retain most or all of the tax raised from what is built in their area, converting new development from a pure local cost into funded local benefits such as town-centre renewal, road repair or council tax cuts.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: The specific mechanism to watch in UK devolution announcements - without revenue retention, devolution headlines don't change building behaviour.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues UK councils have been lumbered with social care and special-needs education - costs driven by demographics they do not control - so any marginal revenue is absorbed before it can fund place-making or economic development.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Explains why UK council finances deteriorate regardless of local economic performance - a persistent credit and service-quality risk at the local authority level.

insights.claim: Charity shops' exemption from business rates lets them outbid commercial tenants for prime high-street positions, which Sam Bowman treats as a distortion and Peter McCormack reads as proof that removing business rates would revive town centres.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman and Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: A visible natural experiment: the tenant mix on UK high streets is a direct readout of business rates policy, not of consumer demand.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues economists systematically under-model inflation's damage because the real harm is the destruction of trust - people lose the ability to plan and feel every counterparty is ripping them off - rather than the relative-price distortion economists usually measure.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Argues the political cost of an inflation episode persists long after CPI normalises, so policy risk stays elevated well past the disinflation.
insights.quote: I think inflation is hugely underestimated by economists

insights.claim: Sam Bowman draws a causal chain from inflation to political extremism: once the implicit deals with businesses, the state and society break down, previously discredited policies return to the mainstream - rent controls being the clearest example, having been off the agenda 15 to 20 years ago.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Gives a leading indicator for post-inflation policy risk: watch which previously unthinkable interventions re-enter mainstream debate.
insights.quote: periods of inflation or high inflation are often followed by periods of incredible political extremism

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's top near-term UK policy risk is rent controls, precisely because they are enormously destructive, hard to unwind, and cost the government nothing - the attractive combination for an administration constrained by borrowing costs with no room for new spending.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific intervention most likely to be reached for by a fiscally constrained UK government and most damaging to UK residential rental assets.

insights.claim: US labour market turnover is roughly ten times Germany's - about 1% of the workforce changes jobs every month in America versus 0.1% in Germany.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A single hard ratio for the dynamism gap that underlies persistent US-versus-Europe earnings and valuation divergence.
insights.quote: 0.1% of the workforce changes jobs every month in Germany. 1% changes jobs every month in America

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues Europe's technology failure is explained by the cost of failure, not the supply of ideas: because firing is expensive - Volkswagen must negotiate with works councils even to close a loss-making plant - experimentation gets located in the US, and the same rigidity now explains German carmakers losing EVs and autonomous vehicles to Chinese and American rivals.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Frames European labour law as the structural driver of the EU's innovation discount, and German autos as the sector where that discount is currently being realised.
insights.quote: failure is so much more expensive in Europe than it is in the US

insights.claim: Peter McCormack relays Charles Goodhart's regime-change thesis from a recent interview - that the decades of exporting production to cheap markets such as China are ending and structurally higher inflation is coming - and Sam Bowman endorses it as entirely right.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host), citing Charles Goodhart
insights.so_what: Two independent voices converging on a higher structural inflation floor argues against mean-reversion assumptions in long-duration UK and European fixed income.
insights.quote: Huge inflation is coming

themes.theme: AI, Energy & the Physical Constraints on Growth

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues AI ends software's exemption from physical constraints: because compute, energy supply and grid reliability directly determine both training and inference quality, a country's ability to build infrastructure now directly gates the quality of AI it can access.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Links the planning and energy reform thesis directly to AI competitiveness - making UK grid and data-centre consenting a tradeable proxy for national AI positioning.
insights.quote: AI is a physical technology. AI requires compute. It requires energy

insights.claim: Sam Bowman takes seriously forecasts that the world will be literally unrecognisable in 18 months, specifically because the people making them previously called the maths capabilities of AI models and frontier-lab revenues close to exactly right.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A track-record-based rather than vibes-based case for short AI timelines, and an argument for weighting forecasters by their prior calibration on revenue and capability.
insights.quote: the world is going to be like literally unrecognizable in 18 months

insights.claim: Sam Bowman's central AI risk is political backlash rather than capability: he expects a war against the machines, and warns that blocking data centre construction over job fears - rather than targeted bio-risk safeguards - is the genuinely damaging outcome.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Locates AI policy risk in local infrastructure consenting rather than in model-level regulation, which is where data-centre and power capex exposure would actually be impaired.
insights.quote: stopping data centers from being built because people are worried about their jobs is crazy

insights.claim: Sam Bowman uses nuclear power as the precedent for AI's likely fate: nuclear was already incredibly safe in the 1950s and 60s and cost-competitive with coal, and it was regulation rather than physics or economics that made it unviable without massive state subsidy.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: A concrete historical template for how a superior technology gets regulated into non-viability - the base case for what AI backlash could cost.
insights.quote: it was competitive with coal in terms of cost

insights.claim: Sam Bowman argues the UK energy consensus has flipped remarkably fast, with net zero going from unanimous agreement a decade ago to a minority position even within the Labour government, where the energy department is now among the last holdouts.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Signals that UK net zero policy is more politically fragile than headline commitments suggest - a directional risk for UK renewables subsidy assumptions.

insights.claim: Sam Bowman identifies the mechanism sustaining costly UK renewables policy: the cost is loaded onto consumer bills rather than the taxpayer, so government faces no fiscal constraint and perceives no limit to further deployment.
insights.speaker: Sam Bowman
insights.so_what: Explains why UK energy costs keep rising independent of fiscal pressure, and why relief requires moving the cost onto the balance sheet where it gets scrutinised.
insights.quote: we put the cost onto bills rather than onto the taxpayer

insights.claim: AI has collapsed the cost of building institutional-grade software: Peter McCormack solo-built a fully integrated football club operating system covering ticketing, payroll, medical records, team selection, media publishing and a fan app in two months, estimating it replaced four years of work by a development company.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete data point on AI-driven disestablishment of SaaS and consultancy pricing power, with named incumbents being displaced by individual builders.
insights.quote: I've genuinely done four years of work on my own in two months

insights.claim: Peter McCormack's AI-built MP fact-checking tool cost roughly £6,000 just to process MPs' last 50 tweets, and he halted it over UK libel exposure - illustrating that for AI-enabled accountability tooling the binding constraints are inference cost and legal risk, not capability.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Suggests the near-term bottleneck for AI-native civic and media products is inference economics and jurisdictional libel law rather than model quality.
insights.quote: about six grand
